To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
heat shock protein- 70 derived from lung cancer cells induces a T cell proliferative response in patients with lung tumors.
HSP-70 isolated from lung cancer tissue is immunogenic in patients with lung tumors, but not in healthy controls, and that the antigenic response is transient.
heat shock proteins ( HSP ) derived from human lung carcinomas are complexed with tumor-specific antigens and are able to stimulate T lymphocytes from cancer patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel vaccine against lung cancer.
the identification of tumor antigens complexed with HSP-60 and HSP-70.
the identification of the antigens complexed with tumor-derived HSP and their role in tumor rejection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HSP-70 from autologous cancer cells are associated with specific antigens and that the immune response against these antigens is transient.
HSP-70 is a tumor antigen, but not a tumor-specific antigen.
the antigenicity in lung cancer is restricted to HSP70 from autologous cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HSP-70 from autologous cancer cells are antigenic and that the immune reaction to them is specific and restricted in time.
the HSP-70 of autologous lung tumors is a good candidate for the development of new vaccines against lung cancer.
the immune system can recognize the HSPs derived from the lung cancer cells and the immune response to the lung cancer cells may be mediated through the immune response to HSPs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immune system is capable of recognizing the tumor-specific HSP70 complexed to tumor antigens, which is the key to developing an immune-based cancer therapy.
HSP70 is a potential target for immunotherapy of lung cancer.
HSP-70 is a good candidate for the development of cancer immunotherapy.
